title: App Manual
summary: Start here before the course: what each tab is for, how a short study session flows, how to type Korean, and the big picture before Chapter 1.

units.title: How to use this app
units.situation: You opened Korean Core Starter and want a simple daily route instead of wandering through every tab.
units.goal: I can choose the right tab without guessing and understand how review, romanization, progress, and backup fit together.

beginnerGuide.title: The six tabs
beginnerGuide.body: Learn is the course path. Practice is review and short drills. Shadow is speaking imitation. Roleplay is guided conversation. Dictionary is the reference. Guide is practical help for Korea and for using this app.

beginnerGuide.title: The main rule
beginnerGuide.body: Do not treat the app like a dictionary database. Use Learn for the next small lesson, Practice for memory, and Dictionary only when a word keeps showing up and still feels unclear.

beginnerGuide.title: How review works
beginnerGuide.body: Items you miss can return through spaced review. The app brings them back after longer gaps so weak words stop disappearing instead of being forgotten after one chapter.

beginnerGuide.title: Studying with a Korean friend
beginnerGuide.body: Open any Roleplay scenario and expand "With a Korean friend?" — it holds a Korean note your friend can read to understand their part, so you don't have to explain the exercise. Speak shows three suggested scenarios each week under Buddy session; they stay the same all week, so you can agree on a time in advance. Your friend does not need to be a teacher: the app explains why each line is natural, so all they have to do is play their part and tell you whether people really say it that way.

beginnerGuide.title: Romanization
beginnerGuide.body: Keep Romaja on at the very beginning. Around Chapter 3, try turning it off for short stretches so Hangul starts doing the work.

beginnerGuide.title: Short spoken forms
beginnerGuide.body: Korean shortens its most common words as soon as people speak: 저는 → 전, 것 같아요 → 거 같아요, 이것 → 이거, 무엇을 → 뭘. These are not slang and not 반말 — they stay just as polite, and you'll meet them in the roleplays and in any Korean message. Chapter 5 has a note that lays them out in one table.

beginnerGuide.title: Progress and backup
beginnerGuide.body: Completion is stored in this browser. Use the backup card in Guide before changing devices, clearing browser data, or studying from another computer.

steps: Open App Manual once and read the study flow.
Open Learn when you want new material.
Open Practice when you want a short session or review.
Open Dictionary when you need a deeper explanation for a word, expression, or pattern.
Open Guide again for real-life Korea tasks, Korean typing, backup, and app setup.
Use Shadow or Roleplay briefly after a lesson when you want the sentence to become speakable.
checkpoints: I know what each tab is for.
I know Romaja is temporary support, not the final reading habit.
I know Practice is for memory, not random busywork.
I know progress lives in this browser unless I export a backup.

units.title: Study flow: short app sessions
units.situation: You want Korean to improve in small daily chunks, like a language app, without turning study into a long textbook sit-down.
units.goal: I can run a 10-15 minute session, finish one useful piece, and know what to ask a Korean friend or native helper later.

beginnerGuide.title: Think in small sessions
beginnerGuide.body: One good session is not a whole chapter. It can be one dialogue, one word chunk, one grammar note, one practice set, or one sentence you can actually say.

beginnerGuide.title: Daily route
beginnerGuide.body: Start with Practice for 3-5 minutes, then Learn for one new chunk, then end by saying or writing one sentence from memory. Stop while the next step still feels easy.

beginnerGuide.title: Chapter route
beginnerGuide.body: Read the warm-up dialogue first so you know the situation. Add only the words that belong to that chapter. Study the grammar note, then use Practice to prove you can choose the form without looking.

beginnerGuide.title: Native helper route
beginnerGuide.body: When a Korean native helps twice a week, bring three things: one sentence you made, one expression that felt weird, and one real-life situation you want to handle. Let the app explain the rule; let the native show what sounds natural.

beginnerGuide.title: When you feel stuck
beginnerGuide.body: Do not restart from Chapter 1. Clear due review, reread the last completed chapter, and try one focused Practice mode. If the same word keeps failing, open its Dictionary page and read the examples.

steps: Practice first: clear due review or run one short drill.
Learn next: continue the next unfinished screen, not necessarily the whole chapter.
Add review carefully: save useful words and expressions, not every item you see.
Produce one sentence: say it, type it, or use Roleplay if the chapter gives you enough pieces.
Mark complete only when the chapter goal feels usable without staring at the explanation.
On native-helper days, ask for naturalness and examples, not a full grammar lecture.
checkpoints: I can study for 10-15 minutes without choosing random tabs.
I know the order: review, new chunk, one output.
I know Dictionary supports learning but does not replace Learn.
I know how to use native help even when the helper is not a teacher.
units.notes: Pronunciation polish can wait until the core sentence habit is steady. For now, the strongest habit is to understand the sentence, recall it, and produce one small version yourself.

units.title: Set up Korean typing
units.situation: You need to type Korean for drills, search, messages, delivery apps, maps, and daily life.
units.goal: I can install a Korean keyboard, switch to it, and use tap-input fallback when I do not have Korean typing ready.

beginnerGuide.title: Why this matters
beginnerGuide.body: Typing Korean lets you search Naver Map, text people, use delivery apps, and complete production drills. The app also gives tap-input fallback for typed answers so you are not blocked on day one.

beginnerGuide.title: iPhone or iPad
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard > Korean. Use the globe key to switch keyboards.

beginnerGuide.title: Android
beginnerGuide.body: In Gboard or Samsung Keyboard, open Languages, add Korean, and choose 2-set Korean. Use the globe or spacebar switcher to change languages.

beginnerGuide.title: Mac
beginnerGuide.body: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Input Sources, add Korean, and choose 2-Set Korean. Control-Space usually switches input sources.

beginnerGuide.title: Windows
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > Time & language > Language & region, add Korean, then switch with Win-Space. Choose the Korean Microsoft IME.

beginnerGuide.title: 2-set in 30 seconds
beginnerGuide.body: Consonants are on the left, vowels are on the right, and final consonants combine automatically. Type ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ and the keyboard builds 한.

steps: Install Korean input for your device.
Practice switching between English and Korean.
Type 한, 국, 어 slowly and watch the blocks combine.
Open Chapter 1 and use the Hangul trainer.
When a typing question appears before you are ready, use the tap-input fallback.
checkpoints: I can switch to Korean input.
I know 2-set Korean uses left-hand consonants and right-hand vowels.
I know the app has a tap-input fallback for typed drills.

units.title: How Korean Works
units.situation: A quick map of Korean before grammar details start.
units.goal: I can explain the ten big ideas that make the first chapters less surprising.

beginnerGuide.title: A five-minute map
beginnerGuide.body: These ten cards explain Hangul, word order, particles, politeness, dropped subjects, numbers, and sound changes before you meet them one by one in the course.

checkpoints: I know Korean verbs usually come at the end.
